title: 10.6 Small Group · Group 1
contentObjective: With my small group, I can look back at my answers from Lesson 1-1, describe how my math biography has changed this year, and recognize ways we are all doers of math — one step at a time, with support.
languageObjective: I can talk through each step out loud using a sentence frame and the lesson's key words.

noticeAndWonder.context: It is the last week of school. Your notebook from September lies open next to today's page — your first math story on one side, and everything you have written since on the other.
noticeStarters: I notice my writing about math ___ .
I notice the problems I can now ___ .
wonderStarters: I wonder how my classmate's story ___ .
I wonder where I will use this ___ .
I wonder what my math story says ___ .

turnAndTalk.question: In September you estimated 20 cars × 4 riders = about 80 Ferris wheel riders per turn. Now, at 6 turns an hour, how many riders per hour — and what tool did you use that you didn't have in September?
turnAndTalk.kernel: 80 riders per turn × 6 turns an hour = 480 riders an hour, using a rate — a tool this year's math added.

stems.es: La rueda de la fortuna lleva alrededor de ___ pasajeros por hora porque ___.

stems.en: I used a ___ this year that I did not have in September.
stems.es: Este año usé una ___ que no tenía en septiembre.

turnAndTalk.extend: The wheel now runs 480 riders an hour. If it operates for 5 hours, how many total riders is that — and how is this calculation an even bigger extension of your September math?

turnAndTalk.question: When you sorted skills into 'I could already do this in September' and 'I learned or grew into this during Grade 6,' what made 'dividing a fraction by a fraction' belong in the growth column?
turnAndTalk.kernel: Dividing fractions, using ratios and unit rates, plotting all four quadrants, and solving one-variable equations are new tools Grade 6 added — not skills from September.

stems.en: Dividing fractions belongs in the growth column because ___.
stems.es: Dividir fracciones pertenece a la columna de crecimiento porque ___.

stems.en: Estimating the Ferris wheel stayed in September because ___.
stems.es: Estimar la rueda de la fortuna se quedó en septiembre porque ___.

turnAndTalk.extend: Pick one skill from the growth column and explain how it changes the way you would solve a problem from September, like the Ferris wheel estimate.
extendStems: Using ___, I could now solve the Ferris wheel problem by ___.
This is different from September because ___.

turnAndTalk.question: In September you decomposed 78.5 as 70 + 8.5. This year you learned 78.5 = 157 ÷ 2 and 50% of 157 = 78.5. How does comparing these show your math story changing?
turnAndTalk.kernel: The same number, 78.5, can now be reached through division and percents — tools that didn't exist in your September toolbox.

stems.es: Mi historia matemática cambió porque ahora puedo escribir 78.5 usando ___, no solo ___.

vocabulary.definition: The story of your relationship with math — and how it has changed over time.
vocabulary.definitionEs: La historia de tu relación con las matemáticas y cómo ha cambiado con el tiempo.
vocabulary.example: In September I dreaded fractions; in June I divide them without fear.

vocabulary.definition: To look back at what you did, felt, and learned, and think about what it means.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Mirar atrás a lo que hiciste, sentiste y aprendiste, y pensar en lo que significa.
vocabulary.example: Rereading your Lesson 1-1 answers and noticing what has changed.

vocabulary.definition: The change between what you could do before and what you can do now.
vocabulary.definitionEs: El cambio entre lo que podías hacer antes y lo que puedes hacer ahora.
vocabulary.example: Then: estimate about 80 riders. Now: also find rates, ratios, and percents.

vocabulary.definition: Trusting yourself to try a problem, even when the first attempt might fail.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Confiar en ti mismo para intentar un problema, aunque el primer intento pueda fallar.
vocabulary.example: Starting a hard problem instead of waiting for someone else to.

vocabulary.definition: The people and places around you — where math shows up outside the classroom.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Las personas y los lugares que te rodean, donde las matemáticas aparecen fuera del aula.
vocabulary.example: Store discounts, bus schedules, game scores, recipes at home.

launch.narrative: This is your support small group for Lesson 10.6. We're going to slow this down and build it together, one step at a time. You can ask a question any time — that's what this group is for.

conceptIntro.heading: Let's build it together — Your math story, one year later
conceptIntro.intro: In Lesson 1-1 you estimated riders on a Ferris wheel, decomposed 78.5, and wrote your math story. The question now is not 'what is math?' but 'how have I changed as a doer of math?' We'll walk through a worked example, try one together, then you'll try a few with hints right there when you need them.
conceptIntro.keyIdea: We are all doers of math and use math in our daily lives. Our math stories continue to grow and evolve as we grow and advance.

iDo.title: Watch me reread my September work
lines: In September I estimated the Ferris wheel: 20 cars with about 4 riders each is 20 × 4 = 80 riders — 'about 80.'
Now I can go further with this year's math: at 6 turns an hour, that wheel moves about 80 × 6 = 480 riders per hour.
Same wheel, same me — but my toolbox grew. That difference IS my math story.

weDo.title: Let's revisit 78.5 with this year's tools
lines: In September we decomposed 78.5 as 70 + 8.5 and 80 − 1.5.
This year we learned new ways to say the same number: 78.5 = 157 ÷ 2.
Find one more way to write 78.5 using something you learned this year.
Sentence frame — say it with me: "The multiples/steps I need are ___ , and the answer is ___ ."

youDo.title: Now you try — with support
lines: Try the practice problems below. The hint button is right there whenever you get stuck — use it, that's smart.
Remember the key idea: We are all doers of math and use math in our daily lives. Our math stories continue to grow and evolve as we grow and advance..

explore.instructions: Quick warm-up together: The September cards come straight from Lesson 1-1 — you were already a doer of math before this year started. The Grade 6 cards are what this year added. After sorting, tell a partner which new skill you have actually used outside of class.

connect.scenario: You and your classmates each wrote about your math stories at the beginning of the school year. Everyone has their own math story, and as you encounter new challenges and experiences, your story might change.
connect.promptQuestion: How does your classmate's end-of-school-year math story compare to your story?
connect.prompt: Describe how your math story has ___ this year, ask a ___ about their story, and then ___ the two to see how they are alike and different.

check.stem: In September you estimated the Ferris wheel as 20 cars × 4 riders = about 80. Which of these uses a tool you did NOT have in September to extend that same estimate?
choices: Multiplying the 80 riders per turn by 6 turns per hour to find a rate of 480 riders per hour
Adding the 20 cars and 4 riders together to get 24
Guessing a completely different, unrelated number
Deciding not to estimate the Ferris wheel at all
check.explanation: 80 × 6 = 480 uses a rate, a tool this year's math added — the September estimate of 20 × 4 could not do this. Adding 20 + 4 or guessing does not use any new math tool at all.

check.stem: Which statement best distinguishes a real comparison of math stories with a classmate from just repeating what you already believe?
choices: Naming something the classmate actually said, plus one genuine similarity AND one genuine difference between the two stories
Writing 'we both got better at math' and stopping there
Copying your own September answer word for word
Skipping the classmate entirely and writing only about yourself
check.explanation: The lesson's check requires reporting something the classmate actually said and naming a genuine similarity and a genuine difference — a vague claim like 'we both got better' does not show that any real conversation happened.

check.stem: A student writes, 'My classmate's story changed the same way mine did — we both feel more confident now.' What is missing from this comparison?
choices: A genuine DIFFERENCE between the two stories, not just a shared similarity
The classmate's full name and grade
The exact date Lesson 1-1 was taught
A drawing of the Ferris wheel
check.explanation: A complete comparison names both a similarity and a difference; this answer only states a similarity, so it does not meet the lesson's check for a complete answer.

connect.modelAnswer: My classmate said that in September he only felt safe in math when he could copy an example, and now he tries problems first and checks the example after. We both got more comfortable being wrong on a first try. But our stories differ: his confidence grew most in equations, while mine grew most in ratios, because I started using unit rates when I shop with my mom.

approaching.stem: In Lesson 1-1 you estimated the Ferris wheel: 20 cars each holding about 4 people. About how many riders was that?
choices: About 80
About 24
About 5
About 400
approaching.explanation: 20 × 4 = 80 — the same estimate you made in September, and it still holds up.
choiceFeedback: That divides 20 by 4 instead of multiplying.
That multiplies as if each car held 20 people.
hints: This is the very first estimate of the year — 20 groups of 4.
Multiply the cars by the riders per car.
approaching.stemEs: En la Lección 1-1 estimaste la rueda de la fortuna: 20 cabinas con unas 4 personas cada una. ¿Aproximadamente cuántos pasajeros eran?
approaching.explanationEs: 20 × 4 = 80 — la misma estimación que hiciste en septiembre, y sigue siendo válida.

approaching.stem: How has your attitude about math changed over the year?
approaching.modelAnswer: In September I thought being good at math meant being fast. Now I think it means sticking with a problem — some of my best work this year came on the second or third try.
sentenceStems: In September I thought math was ___ .
approaching.stemEs: ¿Cómo ha cambiado tu actitud hacia las matemáticas durante el año?

approaching.stem: In September you decomposed 78.5 as 70 + 8.5. Which of these ALSO equals 78.5, using division?
approaching.explanation: 157 ÷ 2 = 78.5, so it is another way to write the same number from Lesson 1-1.
choiceFeedback: 78.5 ÷ 2 = 39.25 — that halves the number instead of rebuilding it.
hints: Which quotient lands exactly on 78.5?
Try doubling 78.5 first.
Double 78.5 first. The number you land on is the one being divided by 2.
approaching.stemEs: En septiembre descompusiste 78.5 como 70 + 8.5. ¿Cuál de estas TAMBIÉN es igual a 78.5, usando división?
approaching.explanationEs: 157 ÷ 2 = 78.5, así que es otra manera de escribir el mismo número de la Lección 1-1.

approaching.stem: How have you used math at home or with your family in new or different ways this year?
approaching.modelAnswer: This year I started comparing prices with unit rates at the grocery store — I figured out which size of cereal actually costs less per ounce, which I never thought to do before Grade 6.
sentenceStems: This year at home I used math to ___ .
That was new for me because ___ .
approaching.stemEs: ¿Cómo has usado las matemáticas en casa o con tu familia de maneras nuevas o distintas este año?

approaching.stem: Which statement matches this lesson's big idea about math stories?
choices: Our math stories continue to grow and evolve as we grow
Your math story was finished when you wrote it in September
Only students with high grades have a math story
A math story never changes once it is written
approaching.explanation: The summary says it directly: we are all doers of math, and our math stories continue to grow and evolve as we grow and advance.
choiceFeedback: September was the BEGINNING of this year's story — today's lesson exists because the story kept going.
Everyone has a math story; being a doer of math is not about grades.
The whole point of comparing September to June is that the story DID change.
hints: Why are you rereading Lesson 1-1 today?
Because something changed between then and now.
Stories grow and evolve — which option says that?
approaching.stemEs: ¿Cuál enunciado coincide con la gran idea de esta lección sobre las historias matemáticas?
approaching.explanationEs: El resumen lo dice directamente: todos hacemos matemáticas, y nuestras historias matemáticas siguen creciendo y cambiando conforme crecemos y avanzamos.
choicesEs: Nuestras historias matemáticas siguen creciendo y cambiando conforme crecemos
Tu historia matemática terminó cuando la escribiste en septiembre
Solo los estudiantes con buenas calificaciones tienen una historia matemática
Una historia matemática nunca cambia una vez escrita

approaching.stem: As a result of what we learned together this year, where do you see math used in your community?
approaching.modelAnswer: I see math at the rec center scoreboard, in the percent-off signs at the store, and in the bus schedule my neighbor reads every morning. After this year I also notice ratios — like the mix on the snowball stand's price list.
sentenceStems: In my community I see math at ___ .
This year taught me to also notice ___ .
approaching.stemEs: Como resultado de lo que aprendimos juntos este año, ¿dónde ves que se usan las matemáticas en tu comunidad?

onLevel.stem: Now stretch the September estimate with this year's math: about 80 riders per turn, 6 turns each hour. About how many riders per hour?
choices: About 480
About 86
About 13
About 800
onLevel.explanation: 80 riders on each of 6 turns is 80 × 6 = 480 riders per hour — a rate, one of this year's tools.
choiceFeedback: That divides 80 by 6 instead of multiplying.
hints: Each turn carries a full load of about 80.
There are 6 turns in an hour.
onLevel.stemEs: Ahora amplía la estimación de septiembre con las matemáticas de este año: unos 80 pasajeros por vuelta, 6 vueltas por hora. ¿Aproximadamente cuántos pasajeros por hora?
onLevel.explanationEs: 80 pasajeros en cada una de 6 vueltas es 80 × 6 = 480 pasajeros por hora — una tasa, una de las herramientas de este año.

onLevel.stem: Percents were new this year. What is 50% of 157?
onLevel.explanation: 50% means half, and 157 ÷ 2 = 78.5 — the very number you decomposed back in Lesson 1-1.
choiceFeedback: 107 subtracts 50 from 157 instead of taking 50 percent.
hints: 50% of a number is half of it.
Half of 157 means 157 ÷ 2.
Check your answer by doubling it — you should land back on 157.
onLevel.stemEs: Los porcentajes fueron nuevos este año. ¿Cuánto es el 50% de 157?
onLevel.explanationEs: 50% significa la mitad, y 157 ÷ 2 = 78.5 — el mismo número que descompusiste en la Lección 1-1.

onLevel.stem: What challenges did you face in math this year, and how did you respond to these challenges?
onLevel.modelAnswer: Dividing fractions was my biggest challenge — my first quiz did not go well. I responded by drawing models before using the rule, and by asking my partner to explain her way. By the next unit I could explain WHY dividing by one-half doubles a number.
sentenceStems: My biggest challenge this year was ___ .
onLevel.stemEs: ¿Qué retos enfrentaste en matemáticas este año, y cómo respondiste a esos retos?

onLevel.stem: Which of these is the strongest evidence that YOUR math reasoning grew this year?
choices: You can explain why a method works, not just follow its steps
You finish worksheets faster than in September
You memorized more answers than before
You stopped making any mistakes
onLevel.explanation: Constructing and explaining reasoning is the growth this lesson asks you to look for — it is what makes the math yours.
choiceFeedback: Speed can grow without understanding growing — it is not evidence of reasoning.
Memorized answers work only on problems you have already seen; reasoning works on new ones.
Nobody stopped making mistakes — growth shows in how you respond to them.
hints: Think about reasoning, not speed or memory.
Which option is about understanding WHY?
Explaining why a method works shows the math is yours.
onLevel.stemEs: ¿Cuál de estas es la evidencia más fuerte de que TU razonamiento matemático creció este año?
onLevel.explanationEs: Construir y explicar tu razonamiento es el crecimiento que esta lección te pide buscar — es lo que hace que las matemáticas sean tuyas.
choicesEs: Puedes explicar por qué funciona un método, no solo seguir sus pasos
Terminas las hojas de trabajo más rápido que en septiembre

onLevel.stem: Ask a classmate about their math story. How has your classmate's math story changed since the beginning of the year?
onLevel.modelAnswer: My classmate told me she used to erase everything the moment it looked wrong. Now she keeps her first attempt and writes the fix next to it, because seeing the mistake helped her on the ratio unit. Her story changed from hiding mistakes to using them.
sentenceStems: At the beginning of the year, my classmate ___ .
onLevel.stemEs: Pregúntale a un compañero sobre su historia matemática. ¿Cómo ha cambiado su historia matemática desde el principio del año?

onLevel.stem: In what areas are you more confident about math now? What are your strengths in math?
onLevel.modelAnswer: I am most confident with ratios and unit rates now — I can set up a table and trust it. My strengths are estimating before I solve, which I already had in September, and explaining my steps out loud, which grew this year.
sentenceStems: I am more confident in ___ than I was in September.
onLevel.stemEs: ¿En qué áreas te sientes con más confianza en matemáticas ahora? ¿Cuáles son tus fortalezas en matemáticas?

practice.commonMistake: Treating your math story as finished — writing the same answers you wrote in Lesson 1-1 instead of looking for what actually changed. The story grows and evolves; a retrospective that copies September has missed the point.

exitTicket.stem: Quick check — you've got this: Which statement best captures this lesson's end-of-year summary of 'Math is Mine'?
choices: We are all doers of math in daily life, and our math stories continue to grow and evolve as we grow
Math belongs only to the students who mastered every unit this year
A math story is written once in September and never changes
Math stops mattering once the school year ends
exitTicket.explanation: The summary makes both claims: everyone is a doer of math in daily life, and our stories keep growing and evolving as we advance.
hints: Look back at the Summarize slide.
It has two parts: doers of math, and stories that keep growing.
Which option keeps both?
